opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the timing is a big part of it. A few years ago, if you told people that large language models were not the path to human-level intelligence, they'd look at you like you were a bit of a crank. Now, a lot of people in the industry, including people who invested heavily in scaling LLMs, are starting to see the limits. You can keep feeding these systems more data and more compute, and they get better at certain things, but they still don't understand the physical world. They can't really plan. They don't have persistent memory in any meaningful sense. And they can't reason in the way that even a cat can reason about its environment.

So when I come in and say, look, we need systems that learn world models, primarily from sensory input like video, that can predict the consequences of their actions, and that can plan to accomplish goals, that message resonates more now than it did before. Investors are smart people. Many of them have been watching the space closely, and they can see that the next big jump isn't going to come from just making the token predictor bigger.

The other thing is that I've been saying the same thing for a long time, and there's a track record behind the ideas. Joint embedding predictive architectures, JEPA, and the work we did at FAIR on things like V-JEPA showed that you can learn good representations of the world by predicting in an abstract representation space rather than trying to predict every pixel. That's a concrete research program, not just a vague vision. So people see there's a path, there's a team that knows how to execute on it, and there's a very large set of applications at the end: robotics, industrial systems, assistants that actually understand context, things like that.

And frankly, I think some investors also like the idea of a bet that's differentiated. Everybody is doing LLMs. If you want exposure to something that could be the next paradigm rather than another competitor in a crowded race, this is an attractive proposition. It's a long-term bet, and I'm very upfront about that. This is not going to produce a product in six months. But the people who've come in understand that, and they're in it for that kind of horizon.

r001.rationale: The response says investors are starting to recognize limits of scaling LLMs, including their weak understanding of the physical world and planning, and that AMI’s alternative vision resonates more as a result.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think there's a growing realization among serious investors that the current paradigm has limits. Everyone has poured enormous amounts of money into scaling LLMs, and the returns are starting to flatten. You can make these systems bigger, you can train them on more text, but they still don't understand the physical world, they don't have persistent memory, they can't really reason or plan in any deep sense. And investors are not stupid. They see that the frontier labs are all converging on essentially the same thing, and they ask themselves: where does the next big discontinuity come from?

So when I come to them and say, look, the path to truly intelligent machines runs through world models, through systems that learn from observation the way a baby or a cat learns, that can predict the consequences of their actions and plan accordingly, that's a story that makes sense to them. It's a contrarian bet, but it's a contrarian bet backed by a research agenda I've been developing and publishing on for years. JEPA, the self-supervised learning work, the objective-driven architecture. None of it is coming out of nowhere.

I also think my track record helps. People remember that convolutional nets were dismissed for a long time before they became the foundation of modern computer vision. There's a certain credibility that comes from having been right about something unpopular before.

And frankly, the timing matters. Five years ago, this pitch would have been much harder because everyone was intoxicated by what scaling could do. Now there's more sobriety. People are willing to fund a longer-horizon effort because they suspect the short-horizon one is running out of road. We're not promising a chatbot next quarter. We're saying this is a multi-year scientific program with a very large payoff if it works, and the investors who came in understand that.

r001.rationale: The candidate says serious investors recognize limits in the current LLM paradigm, including flattening returns and shortcomings, which makes them receptive to LeCun’s alternative vision.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s an appetite for a different approach. A lot of investment has gone into systems based on large language models, and those systems are useful. But there are still fundamental questions about how to build machines that understand the physical world, have persistent memory, and can reason and plan.

The vision for AMI is to make progress on those capabilities. That’s a long-term research ambition, with uncertainty attached to it. But investors don’t need to believe that every technical question is solved. They need to see why the problem matters and why the approach is worth pursuing. If you can build systems that learn how the world works and use that knowledge to plan actions, the range of possible applications is enormous.

r001.rationale: The response says that despite LLM systems being useful, fundamental capabilities remain unresolved, and links that gap to investors’ appetite for AMI’s different approach.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of investors realize that current AI systems are very impressive, but there are important capabilities they’re missing. They don’t really understand the physical world, they don’t have persistent memory, and they can’t reliably reason and plan. Scaling language models alone is not an obvious solution to those problems.

So there is room for a different approach: systems that learn models of the world and use those models to predict the consequences of their actions. That’s the direction of AMI. It’s a longer-term research agenda, with real uncertainty, but the potential applications are enormous. You don’t have to believe language models are going to disappear to believe that something important is still missing.

r001.rationale: The response says investors recognize that current AI systems lack physical-world understanding, persistent memory, and reliable reasoning and planning, and that scaling language models alone may not solve these gaps—motivating receptiveness to AMI’s approach.
